section.title: The Work Resumes
section.sectionRationale: After years of standstill, the word of God through the prophets Haggai and Zechariah rouses the leaders to build again. When the Persian governor Tattenai challenges them, the elders keep working under the watchful eye of their God, give a bold and humble confession of their history, and the matter is referred to Darius. It is one movement: the prophetic word revives the work, and God's providence protects it.
section.thesis: God restarts His stalled work through the preaching of His prophets, and He guards it by His watchful eye, so that even an official inquiry cannot halt the builders whose confidence rests not in their own permits but in the God of heaven.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the prophets stir the leaders and the building resumes, verses 1 and 2; Tattenai's challenge met under God's watchful eye, verses 3 to 5; and the elders' confession quoted in Tattenai's report to Darius, verses 6 to 17.

units.label: The prophets stir the work to resume
units.note: the prophets of God were with them

verses.text: Later, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo {{neba|prophesied}} to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, who was over them.
Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak rose up and began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. And the prophets of God were with them, helping them.

units.label: The challenge met under God's watchful eye
units.note: the eye of their God was on the elders

verses.text: At that time Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates went to the Jews and asked, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?”
They also asked, “What are the names of the men who are constructing this building?”
But the {{ayin|eye}} of their God was on the elders of the Jews, so that they were not stopped until a report was sent to Darius and written instructions about this matter were returned.

units.label: The elders' confession in Tattenai's report
units.note: we are servants of the God of heaven and earth

verses.text: This is the text of the letter that Tattenai the governor of the region west of the Euphrates, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates, the officials in the region, sent to King Darius.
The report they sent him read as follows: To King Darius: All peace.

Let it be known to the king that we went into the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. The people are rebuilding it with large stones and placing timbers in the walls. This work is being carried out {{osparna|diligently}} and is prospering in their hands.
So we questioned the elders and asked, “Who authorized you to rebuild this temple and restore this structure?”
We also asked for their names, so that we could write down the names of their leaders for your information.

And this is the answer they returned: “We are servants of the {{elah-shemaya|God of heaven}} and earth, and we are rebuilding the temple that was built many years ago, which a great king of Israel built and completed.
But since our fathers angered the God of heaven, He delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean who destroyed this temple and carried away the people to Babylon.
In the first year of his reign, however, Cyrus king of Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.

He also removed from the temple of Babylon the gold and silver articles belonging to the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken and carried there from the temple in Jerusalem. King Cyrus gave these articles to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he appointed governor
and instructed, ‘Take these articles, put them in the temple in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be rebuilt on its original site.’
So this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been under construction, but it has not yet been completed.”

Now, therefore, if it pleases the king, let a search be made of the royal archives in Babylon to see if King Cyrus did indeed issue a decree to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. Then let the king send us his decision in this matter.

neba.gloss: To prophesy, to speak God's word. The verb, from the Aramaic section, names the engine of the revival: the stalled work resumes not by new political permission but because Haggai and Zechariah prophesied. God's word, preached, is what raises His discouraged people to build again.

ayin.gloss: Eye. The phrase the eye of their God was on the elders pictures God's watchful, protective providence. His attentive care, not a royal permit, is why the officials could not stop the work while the appeal was pending; God was keeping His own.

osparna.gloss: Diligently, thoroughly, with care; a Persian loanword that recurs through the Aramaic documents of Ezra. Even a foreign governor reports that the work is being done osparna, and later the same word marks how carefully the empire itself will fund and protect it, all under God's hand.

elah-shemaya.gloss: The God of heaven, a favorite title in the Aramaic chapters. Standing before an imperial governor, the elders confess themselves servants of the God of heaven and earth, staking their identity and their building on the sovereign Lord above every earthly power.

basic.context: The temple project had been stalled for years. Then God sends two prophets, Haggai and Zechariah, whose preaching stirs Zerubbabel and Jeshua to start building again. The regional governor Tattenai shows up and challenges their right to build, asking who authorized it and demanding names. But the work continues, because God's watchful eye is on the elders, and Tattenai agrees to let it proceed while he refers the question to King Darius. The elders answer boldly, confessing that they are servants of the God of heaven, that the exile was deserved judgment, and that Cyrus himself had decreed the rebuilding. The question is: what gets God's stalled work moving, and what keeps it safe? God's word and God's watchful care.
basic.hermeneutics: This is narrative that shows, not commands. It highlights how God revives His people, through the preaching of His word, and how He protects them, by His providence. The elders' honest confession models faithful witness. We should not expect governors and archives in our own day, but we should expect that God still works through His word and still watches over His people.
basic.originalLanguages: The revival begins because the prophets neba, prophesied. The reason the work is not stopped is that the ayin, the eye, of their God was on the elders. Even the governor admits the work is being done osparna, diligently. And the builders confess themselves servants of the elah shemaya, the God of heaven.
basic.typology: The prophetic word that raises up the builders points to the living word of Christ that builds His church. God's watchful eye over the elders points to the Good Shepherd who keeps His flock. And the confession of sin met by God's mercy points to the gospel itself.
basic.christ: God's stalled work came back to life through His preached word, and that is exactly how Christ builds His church, by the word of the gospel proclaimed. The watchful eye of God that shielded the builders is the same care Jesus promises His people, that no one can snatch them from His hand. And the elders' confession, owning their sin yet resting on God's mercy through Cyrus, is a small picture of the gospel: judgment deserved, grace given.
basic.god: God is the one who revives and protects. He raises up prophets to move His people, and He keeps His watchful eye on them so their enemies cannot stop the work before its time. He is the God of heaven and earth, sovereign over governors, kings, and archives alike.
basic.crossReferences: Haggai 1 and Zechariah 4 record the very preaching that restarted the work. Zechariah 4:6 says it is not by might but by God's Spirit. And 1 Peter 3:12 echoes that the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous.
basic.oneStory: God's work stalls, and then His word, through His prophets, brings it back to life, while His watchful eye guards it from being stopped. This is how God has always advanced His purposes, and how He builds Christ's church still: by the power of His word and the shelter of His providence.

context.literary: The chapter moves in three quick steps, a spare narrative summary of the prophets' preaching and the leaders' response, verses 1 to 2, a face to face inquiry from imperial officials, verses 3 to 5, and then a single long document, Tattenai's report to Darius, that swallows the rest of the chapter, verses 6 to 17. Verse 5 functions as an authorial aside that briefly steps outside the documentary voice to supply the reader with the chapter's real explanation, the eye of their God was on the elders, a theological interpretation the imperial report itself could never have offered, since Tattenai has no interest in Israel's God beyond due process. The embedded letter is itself a small history within the history, the elders recount the temple's building under a great king of Israel, its destruction for covenant unfaithfulness, and Cyrus's decree authorizing its return, compressing the material of 2 Kings 25 and Ezra 1 into a first person confession addressed to a foreign court. That the reader has already met this history from the narrator's own vantage point in chapter 1 means Ezra 5 offers a second, corroborating witness, an outsider's official file that happens to agree entirely with Israel's own account. The letter's formal opening, to King Darius, all peace, and its closing request for a royal decision follow the same epistolary conventions used in the letters of chapter 4, tying this document to the same imperial correspondence system that had just been used against the builders.
context.historical: Haggai and Zechariah both date their opening oracles to the second year of Darius, around 520 BC, fixing the resumption of building precisely within the reign of the third Persian king this book has named. Tattenai governed the vast Persian satrapy called Beyond the River, the region west of the Euphrates encompassing Syria, Phoenicia, and Judah, and his inquiry follows a pattern well attested elsewhere in Achaemenid administration, where local authorities required documented royal authorization before major building or cultic activity; a later Jewish community at Elephantine in Egypt, for example, would similarly petition Persian officials by letter for permission connected to their own damaged temple, showing that Tattenai's demand for a paper trail was standard imperial procedure rather than special hostility. His question, who authorized you, and his request for names were the ordinary first steps of due diligence a provincial governor owed his superiors, not yet a verdict against the project; notably, he lets the work continue while he waits for Darius's reply rather than halting it immediately, a degree of restraint that the text credits not to Tattenai's goodwill but to God's own watchful protection over the elders.
context.canonical: The events of this chapter are the narrative counterpart to two whole prophetic books, Haggai's oracles and Zechariah's opening visions were delivered in these very months to spur exactly this resumption, so that Ezra 5 functions almost as the historical footnote to both books, telling the reader what happened when the prophets' words actually landed. The eye of their God in verse 5 draws on a recurring biblical picture of divine watchfulness, the Chronicler had already said that the eyes of the LORD range throughout the earth to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him, 2 Chronicles 16:9, and Zechariah, prophesying in this same period, describes seven eyes of the LORD that range through the whole earth as symbols of his all seeing care, Zechariah 4:10, so that the phrase in Ezra 5 is not an isolated idiom but part of a live theological vocabulary this generation was hearing preached. The elders' confession also revives the Old Testament's habit of retelling redemption history as testimony, the same pattern Israel used at the offering of first fruits, reciting a wandering Aramean was my father down through slavery and deliverance, Deuteronomy 26:5 to 9, except that here the recital is addressed to a foreign court rather than to God, turning a liturgical form into a legal defense. And naming Sheshbazzar as the one who first laid the foundation, verse 16, quietly confirms the account already given in Ezra 1:8 to 11, letting an outside document corroborate Israel's own record.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: The writer wants a discouraged, apathetic readership, the very audience Haggai rebukes for saying the time has not yet come, to see concretely what changed their fathers' minds, not better political conditions, since Tattenai's inquiry arrives almost immediately, but the preached word of two prophets. He is equally concerned to answer the fear such preaching provokes once the work resumes and immediately draws official scrutiny; by inserting the theological aside of verse 5 before recounting the details of the investigation, he tells the reader in advance how the story ends, so that the tension of an ongoing imperial inquiry is read through the lens of God's guardianship rather than mere political uncertainty. He also wants the community's public testimony, preserved word for word in the elders' answer, to model how the people of God should identify themselves to power, neither with false humility nor political maneuvering, but as servants of the God of heaven whose history includes both deserved judgment and undeserved mercy.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: The chapter describes one particular resumption of one particular building project under one specific imperial inquiry; it does not prescribe that renewed obedience will always draw official scrutiny, nor that scrutiny will always be resolved this favorably. What transfers is the sequence the passage displays, God's word, preached, precedes and produces God's people's renewed obedience, rather than obedience creating the conditions for the word to be welcomed. It also transfers the manner of faithful testimony under pressure, the elders neither hide their history nor apologize for their present obedience, but state both plainly, trusting the outcome to the God they name rather than to their own persuasiveness. Believers today should expect the same pattern in kind, the priority of God's word in reviving obedience and God's providence in guarding it, without expecting the same historical particulars, governors, archives, or royal decrees.

debates.question: What truly got the work moving again after years of standstill?

views.label: The prophetic word of God
views.case: The chapter credits the resumption to Haggai and Zechariah prophesying; the parallel books show their preaching directly rebuking apathy and promising God's presence, so the primary cause is God's word working on the people's hearts.

views.label: The renewed resolve of the leaders
views.case: Zerubbabel and Jeshua rose up and began to build; human courage and leadership were the visible means by which the work advanced, showing that God's word bears fruit through responsible action.

debates.bearing: Both are true and ordered: God's word through the prophets stirred the leaders, who then acted, teaching that revival comes as God's word moves His people to obedient effort.

debates.question: Why does the elders' answer dwell on their fathers' sin and the exile?

views.label: Honest covenant confession
views.case: They freely admit that their fathers angered the God of heaven and were justly handed over to Babylon; the temple's ruin was deserved judgment, so its rebuilding is sheer mercy, and the confession magnifies God's grace rather than Israel's merit.

views.label: A truthful legal defense
views.case: By recounting the history and citing Cyrus's decree, the elders establish the legitimacy of their building under Persian law; the confession doubles as a documented case that the governor can verify in the royal archives.

debates.bearing: Either way, the answer models faithful witness: it tells the truth about sin and judgment while resting the whole hope of the rebuilt house on the God of heaven and His mercy.

study.originalLanguages: Four more words, alongside the prophesying, the eye, the diligence, and the divine title already noted, carry the chapter's argument. The verb describing Zerubbabel and Jeshua's response to the prophets' preaching, qam, to rise up, is a stock idiom throughout the Aramaic and Hebrew Bible for decisive, unhesitating action, the same verb used of a servant leader stirred to obey a word from God rather than merely feeling encouraged by it; the text is careful to show the prophetic word producing a verb, rising and building, not only a mood. Tattenai's title, pechah, governor, is a Persian administrative term borrowed into Aramaic from an older root for a district officer, and the narrator uses it evenhandedly for both the hostile leaning imperial official and, in the very same verses, for the Jewish leadership recognized under the same title, a detail that quietly shows the returned community operating within, not outside, the empire's own legal categories. The material the builders use, described as large, hewn stone, is a technical building term that appears elsewhere for the costly, finished masonry used in royal and sacred construction, compare the great stones of Solomon's own foundations, 1 Kings 5:17, signaling to Tattenai, and to the reader, that this was no makeshift shelter but permanent, monumental building. And when the elders answer him, they choose a single self designation that frames everything else they say, avedin, servants, from the same root as the Hebrew eved, servant or slave, the word Israel had used of itself under Pharaoh and would use again of the coming Servant of the LORD; standing before an imperial governor, the elders do not claim citizenship, ethnicity, or property rights as their defense, only servanthood to a greater master than Darius. Even the small phrase describing the work's success, that it was prospering in their hands, verse 8, pairs a verb meaning to succeed or prosper with the diligence already named, doubling the vocabulary of thoroughness so that Tattenai's own report, written by a man with every incentive to make the project look suspicious, ends up testifying, almost against itself, to how well and how properly the work was going. Each of these words, taken together, describes a community that rises, builds, serves, and succeeds under a watching God.

typology.type: The prophetic word that raises up the builders
typology.fulfillment: The prophetic word alone, with no new political permission, is what raises a stalled project back to life, and Peter draws the identical connection for the new birth itself, believers are born again through the living and abiding word of God, 1 Peter 1:23, and faith itself comes through the message, and the message through the word of Christ, Romans 10:17. The type is not exact, since Haggai and Zechariah spoke to people already in covenant with God, while the gospel word creates covenant relationship where none existed, an escalation from reviving obedience to creating life itself.

typology.type: The eye of God guarding the elders
typology.fulfillment: The eye of God kept the elders safe through an inquiry they could not control the outcome of, and Jesus claims the same watchful keeping over his own, my sheep hear my voice, and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand, John 10:27 to 28. The difference is permanence, Tattenai's inquiry eventually closed and Darius's decree eventually arrived, a temporary vindication, while the security Jesus promises his sheep has no expiration date and answers to no higher court that could yet overturn it.

typology.type: Sin confessed and met by God's mercy
typology.fulfillment: The elders' confession, that their fathers angered the God of heaven and were justly exiled, followed at once by the fact of a rebuilt house standing on undeserved mercy, is the exile's gospel in miniature. Paul states the same shape for every believer, all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, Romans 3:23 to 24. The type is incomplete on its own, since a rebuilt building could not itself atone for the fathers' sin the way Christ's redemption actually does.

study.christ: When Tattenai demands to know who authorized you to rebuild this temple and presses for the names of the builders, verses 3 to 4, he unknowingly rehearses the same question religious and political authorities would one day put to Jesus, by what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority, Matthew 21:23. Both interrogations assume that legitimate building or teaching requires a credential the questioner can verify and control, and in both cases the true answer lies above the reach of the court asking the question; the elders appeal past Tattenai to Cyrus and, beneath Cyrus, to the God of heaven, just as Jesus answers by pointing past the religious leaders to the authority of heaven itself, Matthew 21:25 to 27. The chapter's small but pointed note that the prophets of God were with them, helping them, verse 2, describes something more than a single sermon that got the project moving; it pictures sustained, ongoing accompaniment through the work, which is exactly the shape of the Spirit's ministry to the church, not merely inaugurating it at Pentecost but continuing to indwell it, so that believers also are being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit, Ephesians 2:22, and are never left to finish the work of building alone, since the Helper Jesus promised will be with you forever, John 14:16. The elders' answer to Tattenai is also a small model of Christian confession before hostile power, they do not deny their history, soften God's judgment on their fathers, or flatter the empire, but state plainly who they serve and let the outcome rest with him, the same posture Jesus commends when he tells his followers not to be anxious about how to answer before governors and kings, for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say, Luke 12:11 to 12. What Tattenai's inquiry could only delay, no human court can finally arrest, since the house Christ builds does not depend on any government's permission slip but on the word and Spirit of the God who authorized it from before the foundation of the world.
study.god: Notice how ordinary the means are by which this God works. There is no vision, no fire from heaven, no audible voice in this chapter, only two preachers, a governor's routine paperwork, and an official letter working its way through an imperial postal system to a distant king; God's rule over the whole affair is visible only in hindsight, in the aside of verse 5 and in the outcome the next chapter records, not in anything that would have looked supernatural to a bystander at the time. This is a God who is fully sovereign while working almost entirely through ordinary human speech and ordinary imperial procedure, which is itself a claim about his character, he does not need spectacle to govern history. His holiness is on display in the elders' own mouths rather than in any judgment scene, since they volunteer, unprompted, that our fathers angered the God of heaven and were justly delivered into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, verse 12; a God who is honored even in his own people's confession of deserved judgment is a God whose holiness they have internalized rather than merely feared. And there is a kind of understated humor in how thoroughly even a skeptical outsider ends up testifying to him, Tattenai's report, written to protect his own position and possibly to build a case against the Jews, instead preserves for the reader an accurate history of God's dealings with Israel and confirms that the work is being done well and honestly, so that a hostile document becomes an unwitting witness to God's faithfulness. He is, finally, the God who grants success and prospering to work carried out in his name even while it remains under official investigation, refusing to make his blessing wait for every uncertainty to be resolved first. This is a God whose sovereignty does not require the absence of scrutiny, opposition, or delay, only his own quiet, watchful presence within them.

crossReferences.note: Haggai's own record of this event states that the people obeyed the voice of the LORD their God and the words of Haggai the prophet and that the LORD stirred up their spirit so that they came and worked on the house, the very obedience Ezra 5 then narrates from the outside.

Zechariah promises Zerubbabel that the temple will be finished not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, and that the hands which laid its foundation will also complete it, naming in advance the very outcome Tattenai's inquiry threatens to prevent.

The psalmist declares that the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him, on those who hope in his steadfast love, that he may deliver their soul from death, the same watchful care that Ezra 5:5 credits for the elders' safety under investigation.

Jesus promises that his sheep will never perish and that no one can snatch them out of his hand or his Father's hand, a permanent version of the temporary protection the eye of God provided the elders while Tattenai's report made its way to Darius.

The Chronicler says the LORD's eyes range throughout the earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him, the same divine watchfulness Ezra credits for the builders' safety, expressed here as active searching rather than passive observing.

Zechariah calls the seven lamps of his vision the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth, preached in these very months, so that the community hearing Ezra 5's report of God's watchful eye had just heard the identical image from a living prophet.

Israel's ancient liturgy for the offering of first fruits required each worshiper to recite a compressed history of slavery, deliverance, and gift of land, the same pattern of confessing God's past dealings that the elders adapt into legal testimony before Tattenai.

Religious leaders demand to know by what authority Jesus acts and who gave him that authority, the same challenge Tattenai puts to the builders, and in both cases the true answer lies with a higher authority the questioners are unwilling to acknowledge.

Paul tells the church that it is being built together into a dwelling place for God by the Spirit, language that echoes the ongoing help the prophets of God gave the builders in Ezra 5:2, not just a single word to start the work but continued presence to finish it.

study.oneStory: Every renewal in this long story begins the same way, not with better circumstances but with God speaking. He spoke light into darkness at creation, spoke to Abraham to set redemption in motion, spoke through Moses to bring a nation out of slavery, and here speaks again through Haggai and Zechariah to raise a stalled remnant off the ground, a small but real instance of the pattern that culminates when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, John 1:14, God's ultimate speech, no longer through a prophet but in a Son. Just as consistently, the God who speaks also watches. His eye rested on Israel throughout the wilderness, on the elders during Tattenai's inquiry, on the exiled and returning generations through every foreign court that could have destroyed them, and Scripture keeps returning to that image of divine attentiveness as a guarantee that history is never actually adrift, even when God's people can see nothing but paperwork, delay, and the whims of distant kings. What is striking about Ezra 5 is how unremarkable the means look from the ground, two preachers, a routine bureaucratic visit, a letter working through an imperial postal system, nothing an onlooker would have called miraculous, and yet the narrator insists this ordinary sequence was exactly how God kept his ancient promise to bring his exiled people home and rebuild what had been destroyed. The same quiet pattern carries the story all the way to its end. God's word will finish gathering his people through the preached gospel, and his watching eye, no longer felt only as protection from a distance, becomes, in the new creation, a face to face nearness where his servants will see his face and need no other light, Revelation 22:4 to 5. The eye that watched over frightened elders becomes, at the very end, the face they are finally allowed to look upon.

quiz.q: What caused the stalled building work to resume?

options.text: The preaching of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, which stirred the leaders to build.
options.note: Verses 1-2 credit the resumption to the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah.

options.text: A new army sent to protect the builders.
options.note: No army appears; it was the prophetic word that moved them.

options.text: The death of all their enemies.
options.note: The enemies were still active, as Tattenai's inquiry shows.

options.text: A fresh decree from Tattenai the governor.
options.note: Tattenai questioned the work; he did not command it to resume.

quiz.q: Why were the builders not stopped when Tattenai questioned them?

options.text: Because the eye of their God was on the elders, guarding the work.
options.note: Verse 5 attributes their protection to God's watchful providence.

options.text: Because they bribed the governor to leave them alone.
options.note: No bribe is mentioned; God's watchful care is the stated reason.

options.text: Because they had a large army to resist him.
options.note: Their security was God's eye upon them, not military strength.

options.text: Because Tattenai supported their cause from the start.
options.note: Tattenai challenged them and referred the matter to Darius.

quiz.q: How did the elders describe themselves and their history to Tattenai?

options.text: As servants of the God of heaven, whose fathers had sinned and been exiled, now rebuilding by Cyrus's decree.
options.note: Verses 11-16 give their honest confession of sin and appeal to Cyrus's decree.

options.text: As an independent nation owing Persia nothing.
options.note: They appealed to Cyrus's authorization, not independence.

options.text: As people who had never done anything wrong.
options.note: They openly confessed that their fathers had angered God.

options.text: As worshipers of the Persian gods.
options.note: They confessed the God of heaven and earth, not Persia's gods.

quiz.q: What did the elders confess about why the first temple was destroyed?

options.text: Their fathers angered the God of heaven, so He handed them over to Nebuchadnezzar.
options.note: Verse 12 owns the exile as God's just judgment on their fathers' sin.

options.text: Nebuchadnezzar was simply stronger than their God.
options.note: The opposite: God Himself delivered them into Nebuchadnezzar's hand.

options.text: It was an accident of history with no cause.
options.note: They name their fathers' sin as the cause, not chance.

options.text: The Persians had destroyed it.
options.note: Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it, as they state.

quiz.q: How does the way the work resumed point us to Christ?

options.text: God revived His work by His preached word, as Christ builds His church by the gospel, and guards His people as the Good Shepherd.
options.note: The prophetic word and God's watchful eye foreshadow Christ's word and care.

options.text: It shows that God's work depends on government approval.
options.note: The work advanced under God's word and eye before any approval came.

options.text: It teaches that prophets are no longer needed at all.
options.note: The point is the power of God's word, now fully in Christ and Scripture.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The word that revives and the eye that guards both point to Christ.

questions: The stalled work revived when God's word was preached. Where in your life or church has a season of drift needed the fresh stirring of God's word, and how might you sit under it again?
The builders kept working because the eye of their God was on them. How does knowing that God is watching over you with protective care change the way you face opposition or scrutiny?
The elders confessed their fathers' sin openly, yet without despair, resting on God's mercy. How can you learn to be honest about sin while still being confident in grace?
Standing before a powerful governor, the elders identified themselves first as servants of the God of heaven. When your identity is tested by the powers around you, what do you lead with?
God overruled an imperial inquiry to protect His people's work. Where do you need to trust God's quiet providence over decisions and authorities beyond your control?

translationNotes.note: Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo are the same prophets whose books date this preaching to the second year of Darius, around 520 BC; their message is preserved in Haggai 1 and Zechariah 1-8.
The eye of their God was on the elders renders an Aramaic idiom for watchful, favorable providence; it is the theological center of the chapter, explaining why the work was not stopped.
Diligently renders the Aramaic osparna, a Persian loanword recurring in Ezra's official documents; it stresses that the work, and later the empire's support of it, was carried out thoroughly.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Ezra 5:1-17, which lies wholly within the Aramaic section (4:8-6:18); key words are marked Aramaic.
